title: IonAnalytics POC: capacity & autoscale scoping
summary: POC scoping to size reserved GPU capacity and define autoscaling & fallback policies. Discussed concurrency, target latency, benchmark plan, burst strategy using reserved + burst GPUs, KV/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, and timeline for a two-week pilot. Agreed next steps: run baseline benchmark, share pricing and sz guide, set up a temporary Redwood Dedicated dev pool, and schedule a 1-hour runbook review.
topics: success criteria (latency p95, throughput, cost targets)
workload sizing (qps, avg tokens, seq length distribution)
security and data residency for POC

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-15 14:00 PDT | Duration: 56m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions), Jordan Kim (IonAnalytics Head of ML), Maya Ortiz (Infra), Leo Park (Product), Anya R. (Security)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick intro — I'm Alex, I'm the AE on this, with Priya and Samir from the eng side. Jordan, Maya, Leo — great to meet you. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Jordan Kim: Good thanks, excited to scope this out. We've got a POC goal to validate perf/cost for our real-time inference use case.
[00:16] Priya Nair: Cool, let's start with success criteria — what would make this POC a win for IonAnalytics?
[00:22] Leo Park: From product POV it is: p95 latency under 300ms for a 256-token response on the main generate endpoint, sustain 120 rps at 50% concurrency spikes, and no more than roughly $0.45 per 1k tokens for the hot path. Quality must match current model within our eval set (we'll share).
[00:38] Jordan Kim: Also reliability: under 0.5% error rate and predictable autoscale behaviour during morning spikes.
[00:45] Maya Ortiz: Security: we need KMS integration, audit logs, and VPC peering for the POC. We'll treat the POC env like a staging security posture.
[00:54] Priya Nair: Great. On the capacity side, can you walk us through expected traffic shape and sequences? avg tokens, cold start concerns, prefix caching usage?
[01:02] Jordan Kim: Sure. Typical request is 80-260 tokens, average 180. Peak QPS is around 120 for the feature we're testing, but we get short spikes up to 300 QPS for 30-120s. About 60% of requests share a common prompt prefix (customer metadata + instructions) so prefix/KV cache will help.
[01:20] Samir Patel: That cache hit ratio helps a lot; it will reduce per-token compute significantly if we can keep KV cache warm. For sizing, are you evaluating a 13B open model variant or larger?
[01:29] Jordan Kim: We're planning to test with a tuned 13B and also compare a quantized 30B for quality tradeoffs.
[01:36] Priya Nair: OK. For the POC, recommended approach is reserved capacity sized for steady-state (approx 120 rps with batching) plus burst capacity to handle spikes. We usually suggest starting with a small Dedicated pool — e.g., 2 reserved A100-eq GPUs — and enable burst nodes that can spin up to 6 GPUs for short windows. The idea is reserved handles baseline plus KV cache, burst covers the 30-120s spikes.
[01:57] Maya Ortiz: So burst capacity is paid on usage only? How do we control cost during unexpected storms?
[02:03] Alex Chen: Correct — burst is usage-based. You can set hard caps on burst instances and configure fallback policies: for example, if burst capacity not available we can transparently fall back to a smaller quantized model (30B quantized) or a lower-cost region, or shed non-critical requests.
[02:19] Leo Park: How fast does burst come up? We can't have 60s cold start for a user-facing flow.
[02:24] Priya Nair: We aim for sub-90s for a full new VM+node, but with warm-pool strategies you can get sub-15s. For POC we'll pre-warm a small burst pool prior to our peak test runs. Also continuous batching and async warmers help.
[02:38] Jordan Kim: What's your recommended autoscale policy (cooldown, scale step) for this workload?
[02:43] Samir Patel: For short spikes we recommend aggressive scale-up with short cooldowns: scale step of 2 GPUs, cooldown 60-90s, and a max burst of 6 GPUs; scale-down should be more conservative — 5-10 minutes to avoid flapping. Use request latency and queue length as signals rather than raw CPU.
[03:00] Maya Ortiz: And how do you route requests between reserved and burst? Is it policy-based?
[03:05] Priya Nair: Yes policy-based. You can route by latency SLO, cost threshold, or customer tier. For POC, we'll route high-priority traffic to reserved first, then spill to burst. We can also configure model-variant fallbacks (e.g., 13B -> 7B or quantized 30B) if burst is exhaust.
[03:20] Jordan Kim: Any notes on quantization tradeoffs? We need to track quality regressions.
[03:24] Priya Nair: Quantized models reduce memory and increase throughput but may alter generation characteristics; for POC we'll run A/B quality evals on the top 50 prompts you share and measure BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics plus human spot-checks. Redwood Optimize can generate recommendations for quantization profiles.
[03:40] Leo Park: For the bench plan, what tests do you recommend?
[03:43] Samir Patel: Baseline perf with no burst (steady 120 rps) for 30m, spike tests with 300 QPS for 2 minutes repeated 6 times, ramp tests, cold-start test where we drain and spin up nodes, and a long-run (3-4h) to observe cost and cache behaviour. We'll instrument token-level latency and per-route cost. We'll also run correctness checks concurrently.
[04:05] Jordan Kim: Sounds good. We'll provide traffic traces and 50 canonical prompts.
[04:09] Maya Ortiz: Regarding network, we need to confirm VPC peering and route tables. We'll also need KMS role for key access and an audit log retention requirement of 90 days for POC logs.
[04:21] Priya Nair: We can support KMS and S3-based audit exports. For 90d retention we'll include that in the POC spec. There might be a small extra for log retention beyond standard.
[04:31] Alex Chen: On cost — rough estimate: with 2 reserved A100s plus occasional burst to 6 GPUs for spikes, estimated POC spend about $6k-$9k for two weeks depending on burst usage. We'll send a more detailed pricing sheet.
[04:44] Jordan Kim: Can we set a spend cap for the POC so we don't exceed budget?
[04:48] Alex Chen: Absolutely — we'll set hard caps on burst and total spend and alert thresholds.
[04:52] Leo Park: Timeline — what does a typical two-week POC look like?
[04:55] Priya Nair: Week 0 (this week): finalize success criteria, sign temporary POC order for reserved capacity. Week 1: provision Dedicated dev pool, deploy model artifacts, run baseline perf and initial correctness checks. Week 2: run stress/spike tests, iterate configs, finalize results and handoff. We'll do a final readout and recommend production sizing.
[05:12] Jordan Kim: That matches our expectations. Can we also test fallback to region B in case of a regional outage?
[05:17] Samir Patel: Yes — we can simulate capacity loss and trigger routing to another region or fallback model. We'll include a failover run in the stress test plan.
[05:25] Anya R.: Quick security question — how are audit logs structured? We need request-level metadata without PII, and we need RBAC for users.
[05:32] Priya Nair: Audit logs include request id, timestamp, route, model, token counts and high-level metadata; we can filter PII, and we support RBAC + SSO/SAML. We'll share the security checklist after the call.
[05:44] Maya Ortiz: For the benchmarking environment, can we use our own model artifacts or do we need to provide a saved checkpoint in a specific format?
[05:51] Priya Nair: We support standard checkpoints; if you have a custom fine-tuned artifact, we'll help validate it. For POC, provide a model tarball or S3 path and container spec if you use custom ops.
[05:59] Jordan Kim: Any caveats about tokenization differences affecting latency?
[06:03] Samir Patel: Tokenization adds a few ms, consistent across runs; we'll instrument end-to-end and model-only latency so you can see breakdown. Also sequence length distribution matters — longer sequences blow up KV state and memory. We'll simulate real lengths from your traces.
[06:18] Leo Park: About fallback policies — what are typical priorities? degrade model -> queue -> reject?
[06:22] Priya Nair: Typical policy: 1) route to backup region, 2) fall back to quantized or smaller model variant for non-critical traffic, 3) queue with TTL, and 4) escalate to rejection only as last resort. You can configure per-route policies.
[06:35] Jordan Kim: Great. Who owns the benchmark scripts and where will results be uploaded?
[06:39] Samir Patel: I'll own the benchmark scripts, share via our private repo link, and upload results to a shared results sheet. We'll tag runs with timestamps and config metadata.
[06:47] Alex Chen: Ok let's capture next steps — Alex will send pricing and POC order, Priya/Samir will provision the dev pool and bench scripts, Jordan/Maya will share traces and confirm VPC/KMS, Anya will send security items.
[06:58] Leo Park: Any blockers on our side? Budget sign-off and legal review for temporary POC terms.
[07:03] Alex Chen: We'll keep the POC terms minimal and scoped — two-week dev pool, usage caps, and an easy exit. Legal can do a lightweight MOU.
[07:12] Jordan Kim: Sounds good. A couple of minor transcriptions notes: sometimes I say LLM names and the auto-transcription swaps them, we will annotate.
[07:18] Priya Nair: No problem — we'll accept corrections.
[07:22] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the pricing sheet and the provisioning timeline by Friday.
[07:27] Jordan Kim: Thanks all.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attribution and small typos expected. Timestamps approximate every ~30-90s.
